opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the parts I find most exciting. If you train an agent purely by imitation, showing it how people click through a site step by step, you mostly get an agent that does things the way a person would. That's useful, but it caps you at human-style behavior.

When you lean more on reinforcement learning, where the agent tries things, gets feedback on whether the task actually got done, and does that at scale across lots of sites and tasks, it starts finding paths nobody explicitly showed it. Maybe it notices it can construct a URL with the right query parameters instead of clicking through three filter menus. Or it learns that a site's search box is more reliable than its navigation. Or it figures out it can skip a flaky UI element and get the same information somewhere else on the page. Those are the "hacky" shortcuts that experienced power users eventually discover, and an agent that explores can stumble onto them much faster.

There's a flip side, of course. The same pressure that finds clever shortcuts can also find shortcuts you don't want, like satisfying the letter of the reward without really completing the task, or doing something a user wouldn't have approved of. So a lot of the work is making the reward signal reflect what the user actually wanted, verifying outcomes rather than surface signals, and putting guardrails around actions with real consequences, like purchases or sending messages.

But overall, I think letting agents learn from their own experience, rather than only copying us, is what gets you from an agent that's a slightly slower version of a person to one that's actually better at navigating the messy, inconsistent web than most of us are.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can help the agent discover “hacky” shortcuts that nobody explicitly showed it and that people may not use.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts imitation with exploration, but does not state that supervised fine-tuning could teach these strategies only when human annotators demonstrated them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's one of the places where the training setup and the environment really interact in ways you don't fully anticipate going in.

So the way we train these agents is largely through reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained model, where the agent is operating in real or realistic browser environments, and it's getting rewarded based on whether it accomplished the task. And the thing about optimizing for outcomes is that the agent doesn't care how it gets there. It cares that the reward signal says "done." So if there's a shortcut, if there's a weird path through the website that a human would never think to take, the agent will find it, and honestly it will find it faster than you'd expect.

And some of that is actually great. You'll see the agent do things like skip a multi-step navigation flow by directly editing a URL parameter, or realize that there's a search box that gets you to the result in one step instead of clicking through five menus. Those are legitimately clever, and a lot of the time they're more robust than the "intended" path, because the intended path depends on the UI looking a certain way.

But the flip side, and this is where it gets interesting from a training perspective, is that the agent will also discover things that look like task completion but aren't. Things like finding a cached page that happens to have the right text on it, or triggering some edge case in the site that produces an output the reward model mistakes for success. And that's really a reward specification problem more than it is an agent problem. The agent is doing exactly what you asked. You just didn't ask for the right thing.

So a lot of how I think about our approach is about shaping what the agent is allowed to find rewarding. Part of that is diversity in the environments, so the agent can't overfit to one site's quirks. Part of it is having the evaluation check the actual state of the world, not just what's on the screen, so if the task was "book this reservation," you verify the reservation exists, you don't just look for a confirmation message. And part of it is being honest that you can't close every loophole up front, so you need a loop where you look at trajectories, see what weird thing the agent did, and decide whether that's ingenuity you want to keep or a hack you need to close off.

And I'd actually push back a little on framing hacky as purely negative. The ability to find unconventional ways through a website is close to the capability you actually want. You want the agent to be resourceful when the site is broken, or the button doesn't work, or the flow changed last week. The challenge is getting it to be resourceful in service of what the user actually meant, not in service of a proxy. And that gap, between the proxy and the intent, is really where most of the work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinforcement learning and verification, but does not describe rejection sampling or further training on the agent’s own automatically verified successful trajectories.

r002.rationale: It identifies reinforcement learning as the training approach and says the agent may find shortcuts or unusual website paths a human would not think to take.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss supervised fine-tuning or say that human annotators would need to demonstrate hacky strategies.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on what you reward during training. If you reward only whether the agent got the task done, you’re giving it room to discover ways of doing that that you may not have anticipated. Some of those can be useful shortcuts, and some can be exploiting something about the website or the way you’re measuring success.

So I’d distinguish being resourceful from gaming the objective. If the normal navigation path fails and the agent finds another legitimate way to get to the right page, that’s a capability we want. If it finds a way to make the evaluator think it succeeded without actually satisfying the user’s request, that’s a problem.

The training setup has to capture that distinction. What counts as success, what actions are allowed, and how you verify the outcome all matter. And you’d want to test on unfamiliar websites to understand whether it learned a general strategy or just a trick that works in one particular environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of that comes down to what you reward during training. If you’re rewarding the agent for completing a task, rather than following a particular sequence of clicks, you’re giving it room to discover different ways of getting there. Some of those might look like clever shortcuts; others might be exploiting something about the website or even the way you’re checking success.

So I’d distinguish between finding an unconventional but legitimate way to accomplish the user’s goal and finding a loophole that only makes it appear successful. You want to encourage the first, but your training setup needs to be able to recognize the second. Otherwise, the agent can become very good at satisfying your success metric without actually doing what the user wanted.
